The author introduces a clinical technique which employs the patient's use of imagination. Patients are asked what they would think of a boss, a caretaker, a coach, etc., who treated them or others in the way that they treat themselves. The patient then focuses on the emotional response they had to a parent or parental substitute and associate it with a bodily zone. This is used to access id impulses of aggression and affection. The discharge of the id and its effect upon the object's representation results in changes in the self-representation and behavior of the patient.

A cursory consideration of the title of this book suggests a tour de force of Dr. Holmes's papers, which promises to reveal insights about the psychoanalysis of women—in itself an enticing aim—but the denotation of the title is in fact much richer and multi-leveled. The book is divided into two parts: “Women” and “Psychoanalysis”; and, even though the primary focus is different in each group of papers, overall Dr. Holmes manages to present throughout an intricate interweaving of developmental theory, clinical examples, and an autobiographical account of her own psychoanalytic coming of age—all the while exhibiting a solid grounding in Freudian theories and feminist criticisms, modern psychoanalytic and object relations approaches. She presents her own theories about the distinctive nature of female development and its place in analysis, providing plenty of examples from her extensive work with individuals and groups, as well as her own personal life experiences. All in all, this intertwining of theory and practice, memories and forward-looking plans, makes for an informative and enjoyable read.

In the book's preface, Dr. Holmes touches on the nature of psychoanalytic training and the qualitative research that it entails. Different Paths Towards Becoming A Psychoanalyst and Psychotherapist: Personal Passions, Subjective Experiences and Unusual Journeys. Arnold Wm. Rachman and Harold Kooden, Editors. London: Routledge, 2021. 280 pp.

Edward Jones

Edward Jones

Edward Jones  

In a collection of revealing and intimate essays, Arnold Rachman and Harold Kooden invite a variety of psychoanalysts and psychotherapists, including the editors themselves, to reflect on the life experiences that preceded their clinical work, and to consider how their familial contexts, unique interests, and even their personal conflicts drew them to the field of psychology 105 and informed their subjective approaches to the work. As one might expect from such a project, the voices and orientations vary considerably. But a common theme emerges, namely that it is possible, perhaps likely or even inevitable, that clinicians will find commonalities between their professional vocations and the disparate passions that precede and run parallel to them. For example, Dan Gilhooley illuminates the similarities between his art practice—the way an image may emerge from the depths of his unconscious only to be understood as such after the fact—and the intersubjective field that arises between analyst and analysand. Similarly, Robert J. Marshall observes affinities between his love of both writing and jazz improvisation on the piano, and his spontaneity and creativity in session with his patients: “The similar styles, while in different realms, namely writing, conducting psychoanalysis, and improvising jazz, seem to stem from a common source and follow a similar common pathway” (p. 115). Each chapter contains such links between the author's earlier life and their work in the treatment room.

These lively, confessional accounts will be of interest to any reader appreciative of memoir as they often function as vignettes within that genre. Likewise, readers with a lay interest in psychology will appreciate the glimpse of “the other side of the couch,” to borrow Kooden's oft-repeated phrase. Any patient who has regarded their therapist as the cliche of objectivity, a “myth” that Phyllis Meadow (1987) notably explored in the pages of this very journal, will find much to suggest the human behind their screen of projections and transferences. But the clinician may be most affected by the implicit suggestion to do their own rumination on the path they took to becoming an analyst. My own master's thesis (Jones, 2019) explores my personal Buddhist and yogic practices as a conduit to understanding modern psychoanalytic technique.

Midlife: Humanity's Secret Weapon, By Andrew Jamieson. Notting Hill Editions Ltd. 2022. 144 pp.

Adam Pollock

Adam Pollock

Adam Pollock  

Andrew Jamieson, a practicing psychotherapist and orchestral concert promoter in the UK, has written a short book, handsomely turned out in red cloth by Notting Hill Editions, on the human potential coiled in the midlife crisis. In his practice, he writes, three-fourths of his clients have been between their thirties and fifties, arriving in a “state of near breakdown,” anxious, depressed, and beset by the feeling that they've lost their way (p. 1). Having both seen and been versions of this patient, I can affirm that this is territory worthy of exploration. For Jamieson, midlife is an essential developmental phase. Refreshingly, he does not couple it to procreation. Instead, it's a phase of personal emotional development through introspection. Its task is one of “ethical evolution,” to balance out the tumult and destructiveness of our technological evolution (p. 4). Engaging with the work of midlife is good for the individual, plausibly essential for human survival; the stakes are nuclear. Jamieson makes his case through a loose, intermodal theoretical structure and a set of personal and historical exemplars. It's the midlife crisis theory of Great Men, and a few women.

Jamieson admires Jung, and has studied his work and life. He thinks in terms of shadow and anima, egocide and individuation. At the Risk of Thinking: An Intellectual Biography of Julia Kristeva By Alice Jardine. Edited by Mari Ruti. New York: Bloomsbury Academic, 2020. 400 pp.

Michal Tziyon

Michal Tziyon

Michal Tziyon  

At the Risk of Thinking: An Intellectual Biography of Julia Kristeva is a biography of the renowned philosopher, semiotician, psychoanalyst, novelist, activist and prolific writer. This biography is authored by Alice Jardine, professor of French literature, post-structuralist and feminist theory and Studies of Women, Gender and Sexuality at Harvard University. Jardine first met 215 Kristeva at Columbia University when she was a student there in the 1970's and was Kristeva's research assistant. This was the beginning of a professional and personal relationship that has spanned decades. The book was edited by Mari Ruti, Distinguished Professor of Critical Theory, Gender and Sexuality Studies at the University of Toronto.

Prior to reading this biography, I encountered Kristeva's work through two of her 45 books, Black Sun (1987), a book about depression, and Powers of Horror (1980), an exploration of power and otherness, which introduces the concept of “abjection.” In my search to make sense of myself as a mother of very young children this concept made a lasting impression on me. “Abjection” originated in Kristeva's own experiences as a mother of an infant, and as she returned to Klein and Freud, she found the origins and fear of the “other” and the “foreign” as originating in the pre-oedipal stage “where there is no subject, no object, just attraction and rejection.” This instability between subject and object exists between mother and infant:

This in between state that pulls us in through fascination but then makes us want to spit it out can become frightening. In the adult subject it can lead to the kind of defensiveness… the desire to no longer live “at the border” but to retreat within, to defend oneself (and those like oneself), and to exile (when not to eradicate) the scapegoat seen as causing the invasion of impurity. (p. 196)

Kristeva applied this concept in her study of Louis-Ferdinand Céline, a famed French novelist (1894-1961) and an antisemite who advocated alliance with Nazi Germany, “thereby illustrating an instability between self and other that is found at the core of all racism” (p. 196).

Errors are a part of life and clinical mistakes are frequent. The author examines some of the ways that errors or mistakes permeate all areas of life, pointing out their frequency in human interaction, in research, in ordinary judgment, whether in daily largely trivial matters, or in significant matters of life and death. In some instances, a psychoanalyst might point out an unconscious motive for the errors, but in the history of psychoanalysis, clinical errors have often been shown to be beneficial to the treatment, to the extent that they enter into the psychoanalytic discourse. The author presents some clinical material drawn from his own work with two supervisees.

Elena Molinari MD PHD

Elena Molinari

Email: eleni.molinari@gmail.com

Elena Molinari   Physician specialized in pediatrics and psychotherapy, with expertise in child and adolescent psychoanalysis. She is a member of the Italian Psychoanalytic Society (SPI) and she has taught child neuropsychiatry for the postgraduate course in art therapy at the Academy of Fine Arts of Brera in Milano since 2004. She has published several papers in international reviews and made contributions to various collective books. She is the author of Field Theory in Child and Adolescent Psychoanalysis: Understanding and Reacting to Unexpected Developments (Routledge, 2017), a book that reflects on Bion's theories applied to child analysis.

Bion postulated that the unconscious develops from the capacity to dream. Expanding his interest in the psychotic functioning of the mind, he wrote that alongside conscious and unconscious states of mind, there is a third psychic category: the inaccessible unconscious. He relates this mental category to the most archaic memory traces, including those related to earliest traumas registered only in non-representational form. During a mother-child therapy, with a profoundly traumatized mother, the author observes how the mother's lack of psychic containment increased the expression of the child's emotions through disharmonious and untargeted body movements. The author offers channels for nonverbal communication based on identifying the distortion in this very primitive formal layer of experience. Thinking of the baby's movements and presymbolic expressions as nascent “dreams,” the author uses them in session to share something of the mother's “ontological anxiety” with her, communicating them as a “selected fact,” potentially useful in catching something of the mother's inaccessible unconscious and unavailability.

Group Analysis During COVID-19

Jane Goldberg PHD

Jane Goldberg

Email: janegoldberg@janegoldbergphd.com

Jane Goldberg   Practicing psychoanalyst for over 50 years, specializing in the fields of psychological oncology and mind/body health. She is the founder of holistic wellness centers located in New York City, Puerto Rico, and soon to be expanded to New Jersey. Her latest book is The Hormesis Effect, and she is currently completing a companion set of publications: The Revolutionary Mind Project and The Evolutionary Brain Project.

During COVID-19, the author, like most psychoanalysts and psychotherapists, was forced to move her practice from in-person to a digital platform (Zoom). Although her initial expectation was that much of the therapeutic value of the group experience would be diminished, she was surprised that the contrary proved to be evident: Her pre-existing groups flourished, and there appeared to be no loss in efficacy based on member self-report data. The author makes the case that group analysis is essential to a comprehensive analytic experience and not an addendum to individual analysis. The author explores her theoretical positions and provides personal commentary from some of her patients on the transition to and experience of in-person versus telehealth options.

Speaking the Never Spoken: The Challenge of id Analysis**

Mary Shepherd Psya.D.

Mary Shepherd

Email: maryshepherd@comcast.net

Mary Shepherd   One of the founders of the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis (BGSP), the only free-standing institution granting graduate degrees in psychoanalysis. Dr. Shepherd has written a number of articles expanding and elaborating the basic concepts in Modern Psychoanalysis. She claimed in her 2008 article, “The Silent Revolution in Psychoanalysis: Hyman Spotnitz and the Reversibility of Schizophrenia,” that Spotnitz' advances in technique constituted a revolution in the field, opening psychoanalytic cure to all diagnoses. She is a training and supervising analyst at BGSP and has a private practice in Cambridge, MA.

This paper grapples with the complexities of helping patients verbalize material never before verbalized, material trapped in the id impulses that form the rigid neuronal pathways of the repetition compulsion. André Green, Hyman Spotnitz, and a sampling of neuroscientists provide the conceptual basis for examining this critical psychoanalytic task.

A waking Dream: Condensation and Symbolism in Bob Dylan's Murder Most Foul**

Barbara D'Amato PsyaD LP

Barbara D'Amato

Email: drbarbaradamato@gmail.com

Barbara D'Amato   Faculties of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies (CMPS) and the New York Graduate School of Psychoanalysis (NYGSP). She is director of the CMPS Distance Learning Program. She has had an interest in dreams and dreaming for many years, presenting internationally and writing extensively on literary authors and their dreams, the function of aggression in dreams, and the modern psychoanalytic approach to working with dreams. She is in private practice in New York City; Bay Ridge and Union Square.

Approaching Bob Dylan's Murder Most Foul as a waking dream, the author interprets the words, imagery and symbolism apparent from the songwriter's life and decades of social commentary. Using Freudian, modern and contemporary psychoanalysis she attempts to understand Dylan's lyrics through her own subjective experience.

Mindblow, Ludovico and the Melody of Things**

Sara Boffito

Sara Boffito

Email: sboffito@hotmail.it

Sara Boffito   IPA Psychoanalyst and member of the Italian Psychoanalytic Society. She is an IPA expert in child and adolescent psychoanalysis. Along with being Associate Editor of the International Journal of Psychoanalysis, she is also a member of the editorial board for Rivista di Psicoanalisi (Journal of the Italian Psychoanalytic Society) and for the COWAP IPA Book Series (Routledge). Besides publishing and presenting several works in international journals, congresses and collective books, she also translates foundational English language authors of psychoanalysis into Italian.

An 11 year-old boy with autism and primitive fears builds a transference to his analyst through drawing, music and storytelling. The analyst's initial countertransference feelings clue her in to his premature birth and his desperate need for containment. Through the informed manner in which the analyst works, the child evolves his mind by contacting the analyst's internal experiences when he makes music. The analytic pair “keeps time” by developing rhythms, language and songs, despite the interruption of the COVID-19 lockdown.

Just Below the Surface: The Creative Expression of Psychosomatic Symptoms

Michael Sendrow

Michael Sendrow

Email: msendrow@cmps.edu

Michael Sendrow   Recent graduate of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies (CMPS), with an M.A. from the New York Graduate School of Psychoanalysis (NYGSP). Since earning his B.A. in English and Theatre Arts from the University of Pennsylvania, creative expression — namely, fiction and personal essays — has played a central role in his self-analysis and, now, in his psychoanalytic research. He works in private practice in New York City.

While working with patients who seek treatment for physical symptoms that appear to defy traditional medical remedy, a unique opportunity arises to observe and interpret unconscious fantasy. The author examines his own history of somatic disorder in parallel with one such patient, whose pain syndrome inhibits everyday functioning. Using their shared artistic identities, the author then explores the uses of psychosomatic symptomatology as both a substitute for and obstacle to creative expression.
